The specification defines grip vacuum as a positive magnitude so that "greater than" and "falls to" mean exactly one thing throughout, and FIG. 4 plots the three levels and dimensions the resulting warning interval.

1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
12	
13	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a warning is given, it is given either on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
14	
15	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
16

1	This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.
2	
3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which, when placed against a workpiece, bounds a sealed region between the suction cup and the workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air from the sealed region through a port so as to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region, the grip vacuum holding the suction cup, and hence a load carried by the suction cup, against the workpiece. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is carried by the rigid body and is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the electric vacuum pump.
4	
5	The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure in the sealed region is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.
6	
7	The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is not the level at which the grip fails and is not the level at which the pump is asked to run again. It is a level that is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is above the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still holding the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told. That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.
8	
9	This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level, rather than with respect to the working vacuum level or with respect to a rate of change, is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.
10	
11	In embodiments, the warning indicator remains active for as long as the grip vacuum stays at or below the warning vacuum level, so that a grip which is decaying continuously produces a warning which persists rather than a single transient. In embodiments, the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle and whose eyes are on the panel. In embodiments, the pressure sensor is in fluid communication with the sealed region, so that what is monitored is the grip vacuum acting on the workpiece itself rather than a proxy elsewhere in the machine.
12	
13	Because the electric vacuum pump, the pressure sensor, the warning indicator, and the rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without any hose, cord, or external controller, and can be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand.
14	
15	A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air from the sealed region with the electric vacuum pump to establish the grip vacuum, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is carried, and activating the warning indicator when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level.
16

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the absolute pressure within the sealed region 18 is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is removed from the sealed region 18 and falls as air leaks back into it. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the pressure difference clamping the suction cup 10 to the workpiece 50 is larger, and that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.
4	
5	The release vacuum level 66 is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying, that is, the grip vacuum at which the holding force produced across the area bounded by the flexible sealing lip 12 ceases to exceed the force tending to separate the suction cup 10 from the workpiece 50. The release vacuum level 66 is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and orientation in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The warning vacuum level 64, by contrast, is a property of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100: it is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
6	
7	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. In the illustrated embodiment the handle 16 is an arch standing above an upper side of the rigid body 14 and the suction cup 10 depends from a lower side of the rigid body 14, so that the whole of the load hangs below the user's hand and the line of action of the load passes through the handle 16. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit: no hose, no cord, and no external controller is connected to it in use.
8	
9	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not give the outside dimensions of the rigid body 14, the diameter of the suction cup 10, the rated load, or the materials of the rigid body 14 and the flexible sealing lip 12. Please supply these; a filing-quality description would ordinarily state at least a working size range for the suction cup 10, the rated load it is designed to carry, and the elastomer used for the flexible sealing lip 12.]
10	
11	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12 which projects toward the workpiece 50 and runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50, and the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face of the workpiece 50 together bound a sealed region 18. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the only part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows the sealed region 18 to be closed against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.
12	
13	An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air from the sealed region 18 through a port 22. The port 22 opens into the sealed region 18 through the suction cup 10, and a suction passage 24 within the rigid body 14 connects the port 22 to an inlet of the electric vacuum pump 20. Air drawn from the sealed region 18 is discharged to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet 26 in the rigid body 14. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air from the sealed region 18 and so raises the grip vacuum; the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50.
14	
15	Because the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 rather than mounted remotely and connected by a hose, the whole of the evacuated volume is short and small: it consists of the sealed region 18, the port 22, and the suction passage 24. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described below, because it means that a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall in the grip vacuum rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.
16	
17	A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. In the illustrated embodiment the pressure sensor 30 is in fluid communication with the sealed region 18 by way of a sensing passage 34 that branches from the suction passage 24 on the sealed-region side of the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the pressure sensor 30 sees the pressure in the sealed region 18 itself and not a pressure developed elsewhere in the machine. What is monitored is thus the grip actually acting on the workpiece 50.
18	
19	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure states that the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum but does not state where it is plumbed or what type of sensor it is. The sensing passage 34 branching from the suction passage 24 is described here as one way to give the pressure sensor 30 sight of the sealed region 18. Please confirm the sensing location (sealed region, port, suction passage, or pump inlet) and the sensor type (for example piezoresistive gauge-pressure transducer, or a pressure switch with a fixed trip point), and supply the sensing range.]
20	
21	A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The warning indicator 32 is placed on the rigid body 14 where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle 16 and whose attention is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool.
22	
23	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not state the modality of the warning indicator 32 - whether it is visual, audible, vibratory, or a combination. Please confirm which are supported, so that the description and the corresponding dependent claim can be made specific. Nothing in this description should be read as an assertion that a particular modality was disclosed.]
24	
25	The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 over a drive path 36 that includes a threshold circuit 38. The threshold circuit 38 compares the grip vacuum reported by the pressure sensor 30 with the warning vacuum level 64 and energizes the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum has fallen to the warning vacuum level 64.
26	
27	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure states that the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 but does not state how the comparison against the warning vacuum level 64 is implemented. The threshold circuit 38 is described here generically. Please confirm the implementation - a discrete comparator, a microcontroller executing firmware, or a pressure sensor with an integral threshold output - and whether the warning vacuum level 64 is fixed at manufacture or user-adjustable. If it is adjustable, the adjustment means and range are needed.]
28	
29	A rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20 over a power path 44. The rechargeable battery 40 also supplies the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 over the power path 44, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand. A charging interface 42 on the rigid body 14 receives charging power for the rechargeable battery 40 from an external source between uses.
30	
31	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not state the battery chemistry, voltage, capacity, whether the rechargeable battery 40 is removable or internal, or the form of the charging interface 42. Please supply. Also, the disclosure does not describe the user controls by which the electric vacuum pump 20 is started and by which the grip is released at the end of a lift; a filing-quality description needs them, and no such controls have been invented here.]
32	
33	FIG. 3 shows the same arrangement schematically. Air is drawn from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and the suction passage 24 by the electric vacuum pump 20 and discharged through the exhaust outlet 26. The pressure sensor 30 is coupled to the sealed region 18 by the sensing passage 34 and is coupled to the warning indicator 32 by the drive path 36 through the threshold circuit 38, the threshold circuit 38 comparing the monitored grip vacuum with the warning vacuum level 64. The rechargeable battery 40 feeds the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, and the warning indicator 32 over the power path 44 and is replenished through the charging interface 42. Everything in FIG. 3 is carried by the rigid body 14.
34	
35	The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays.
36	
37	The electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to a working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect - because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50 - air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.
38	
39	Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.
40	
41	The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.
42	
43	This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning "the grip is failing and you still have hold of the panel." It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.
44	
45	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip - a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
46	
47	In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates only when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.
48	
49	In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 at the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on the state of the electric vacuum pump 20. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.
50	
51	In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.
52	
53	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not give numerical values for the working vacuum level 62, the warning vacuum level 64, or the design margin between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66, nor the rated load or the expected duration of the warning interval 68. Values, or at least a design rule for setting the warning vacuum level 64 (for example, as a stated fraction of the working vacuum level 62, or as a stated multiple of the release vacuum level 66 computed for the rated load), are needed to support numerical dependent claims. None have been invented here.]
54	
55	In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: such panels are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.
56	
57	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and establishes the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.
58	
59	At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At a comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At a maintaining step 212, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down.
60	
61	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.
62

Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning "the grip is failing and you still have hold of the panel." It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip - a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates only when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.

In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 at the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on the state of the electric vacuum pump 20. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not give numerical values for the working vacuum level 62, the warning vacuum level 64, or the design margin between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66, nor the rated load or the expected duration of the warning interval 68. Values, or at least a design rule for setting the warning vacuum level 64 (for example, as a stated fraction of the working vacuum level 62, or as a stated multiple of the release vacuum level 66 computed for the rated load), are needed to support numerical dependent claims. None have been invented here.]

In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: such panels are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and establishes the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.

At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At a comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At a maintaining step 212, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter has a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. A flexible sealing lip of the suction cup bounds a sealed region against a workpiece such as a glass or stone panel. An electric vacuum pump within the rigid body draws air from the sealed region through a port to establish a grip vacuum that retains a load, a pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum, and a rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the pump. A warning indicator on the rigid body, driven by the pressure sensor, activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level that is greater than the release vacuum level at which the suction cup would let go, so the user is warned while the cup is still holding the load.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the absolute pressure within the sealed region 18 is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is removed from the sealed region 18 and falls as air leaks back into it. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the pressure difference clamping the suction cup 10 to the workpiece 50 is larger, and that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.
4	
5	The release vacuum level 66 is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying, that is, the grip vacuum at which the holding force produced across the area bounded by the flexible sealing lip 12 ceases to exceed the force tending to separate the suction cup 10 from the workpiece 50. The release vacuum level 66 is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and orientation in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The warning vacuum level 64, by contrast, is a property of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100: it is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
6	
7	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. In the illustrated embodiment the handle 16 stands above an upper side of the rigid body 14 as an arch and the suction cup 10 depends from a lower side of the rigid body 14, so that the whole of the load hangs below the user's hand and a line of action of the load passes through the handle 16. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle 16 and whose attention is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. An exhaust outlet 26 in a side wall of the rigid body 14 is the opening through which the air drawn from the sealed region 18 is discharged to atmosphere. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit that is used unconnected to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.
8	
9	FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which projects toward the workpiece 50 and runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50, and the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face of the workpiece 50 together bound a sealed region 18. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the only part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows the sealed region 18 to be closed against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.
10	
11	An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air from the sealed region 18 through a port 22. The port 22 opens into the sealed region 18 through the suction cup 10, and a suction passage 24 within the rigid body 14 connects the port 22 to an inlet of the electric vacuum pump 20. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air from the sealed region 18 and so raises the grip vacuum; the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14, to the workpiece 50.
12	
13	Because the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 rather than mounted remotely and connected by a hose, the whole of the evacuated volume is short and small: the volume evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 consists of the sealed region 18, the port 22, and the suction passage 24. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described below, because it means that a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall in the grip vacuum rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.
14	
15	FIG. 3 shows the sensing, warning, and power arrangement of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. In the illustrated embodiment the pressure sensor 30 is in fluid communication with the sealed region 18 by way of a sensing passage 34 branching from the suction passage 24 of FIG. 2 on a sealed-region side of the electric vacuum pump 20 and connecting the suction passage 24 to the pressure sensor 30, so that the pressure sensor 30 sees the pressure in the sealed region 18 itself and not a pressure developed elsewhere in the machine. What is monitored is thus the grip actually acting on the workpiece 50.
16	
17	The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 over a drive path 36 connecting the pressure sensor 30 to the warning indicator 32, the drive path 36 comprising a threshold circuit 38. The threshold circuit 38 is configured to compare the grip vacuum monitored by the pressure sensor 30 with the warning vacuum level 64 and to energize the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum has fallen to the warning vacuum level 64.
18	
19	A rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20 over a power path 44. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 over the power path 44, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand. A charging interface 42 on the rigid body 14 is configured to receive charging power for the rechargeable battery 40 from a source external to the rigid body 14 between uses.
20	
21	The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays.
22	
23	The electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to a working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.
24	
25	Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The warning indicator 32 is thus configured to activate before the load can be dropped. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68. The warning interval 68 begins when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 and ends when the grip vacuum falls to the release vacuum level 66.
26	
27	The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Setting the workpiece 50 down during the warning interval 68 ends the lift without a drop. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.
28	
29	This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the panel is still held. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.
30	
31	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip, such as a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
32	
33	Carrying the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the warning indicator 32, and the rechargeable battery 40 on the rigid body 14 is what makes that window available at all, and it solves a problem that a tethered arrangement cannot. A lifter that took its vacuum through a hose, its power through a cord, or its decision from a controller external to the rigid body 14 would put part of the chain that has to react to a failing seal somewhere other than in the user's hand. Length of hose between a remote vacuum source and the suction cup 10 adds evacuated volume, and, for the reason given above, added evacuated volume buffers a leak and slows the fall in grip vacuum that the pressure sensor 30 has to see. A decision taken off the tool has to be carried back to the user over the same tether, and the tether is itself what stops the tool from going up a ladder or onto a scaffold. Because the sealed region 18 is evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 within the rigid body 14, is watched by the pressure sensor 30 carried by the rigid body 14, and is reported by the warning indicator 32 carried by the rigid body 14, all of them powered by the rechargeable battery 40 carried by the rigid body 14, the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 establishes the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14. The whole chain, from the seal that is failing to the person who must act on it, is in the one hand that is holding the load.
34	
35	In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.
36	
37	In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on the state of the electric vacuum pump 20. When a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.
38	
39	In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.
40	
41	In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being configured to conform to and seal against a face of the panel under a clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: such panels are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.
42	
43	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 so as to establish the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.
44	
45	At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At a comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At a maintaining step 212, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down. The placing step 202, the evacuating step 204, the monitoring step 206, the comparing step 208, the activating step 210, and the maintaining step 212 are all performed with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 unconnected to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.
46	
47	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.
48

In the illustrated embodiment the handle 16 stands above an upper side of the rigid body 14 as an arch and the suction cup 10 depends from a lower side of the rigid body 14, so that the whole of the load hangs below the user's hand and a line of action of the load passes through the handle 16. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16. A warning indicator 32 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is positioned on the rigid body 14 so as to be perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle 16 and whose attention is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool. An exhaust outlet 26 in a side wall of the rigid body 14 is the opening through which the air drawn from the sealed region 18 is discharged to atmosphere. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit that is used unconnected to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which projects toward the workpiece 50 and runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50, and the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face of the workpiece 50 together bound a sealed region 18. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the only part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows the sealed region 18 to be closed against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air from the sealed region 18 through a port 22. The port 22 opens into the sealed region 18 through the suction cup 10, and a suction passage 24 within the rigid body 14 connects the port 22 to an inlet of the electric vacuum pump 20. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air from the sealed region 18 and so raises the grip vacuum; the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14, to the workpiece 50.

Because the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 rather than mounted remotely and connected by a hose, the whole of the evacuated volume is short and small: the volume evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 consists of the sealed region 18, the port 22, and the suction passage 24. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described below, because it means that a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall in the grip vacuum rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.

FIG. 3 shows the sensing, warning, and power arrangement of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. In the illustrated embodiment the pressure sensor 30 is in fluid communication with the sealed region 18 by way of a sensing passage 34 branching from the suction passage 24 of FIG. 2 on a sealed-region side of the electric vacuum pump 20 and connecting the suction passage 24 to the pressure sensor 30, so that the pressure sensor 30 sees the pressure in the sealed region 18 itself and not a pressure developed elsewhere in the machine. What is monitored is thus the grip actually acting on the workpiece 50.

The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 over a drive path 36 connecting the pressure sensor 30 to the warning indicator 32, the drive path 36 comprising a threshold circuit 38. The threshold circuit 38 is configured to compare the grip vacuum monitored by the pressure sensor 30 with the warning vacuum level 64 and to energize the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum has fallen to the warning vacuum level 64.

A rechargeable battery 40 is carried by the rigid body 14 and is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20 over a power path 44. The rechargeable battery 40 is further configured to power the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 over the power path 44, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand. A charging interface 42 on the rigid body 14 is configured to receive charging power for the rechargeable battery 40 from a source external to the rigid body 14 between uses.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to a working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.

Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The warning indicator 32 is thus configured to activate before the load can be dropped. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68. The warning interval 68 begins when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 and ends when the grip vacuum falls to the release vacuum level 66.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68 the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Setting the workpiece 50 down during the warning interval 68 ends the lift without a drop. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the panel is still held. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip, such as a second vacuum source, a reservoir, or an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

Carrying the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the warning indicator 32, and the rechargeable battery 40 on the rigid body 14 is what makes that window available at all, and it solves a problem that a tethered arrangement cannot. A lifter that took its vacuum through a hose, its power through a cord, or its decision from a controller external to the rigid body 14 would put part of the chain that has to react to a failing seal somewhere other than in the user's hand. Length of hose between a remote vacuum source and the suction cup 10 adds evacuated volume, and, for the reason given above, added evacuated volume buffers a leak and slows the fall in grip vacuum that the pressure sensor 30 has to see. A decision taken off the tool has to be carried back to the user over the same tether, and the tether is itself what stops the tool from going up a ladder or onto a scaffold. Because the sealed region 18 is evacuated by the electric vacuum pump 20 within the rigid body 14, is watched by the pressure sensor 30 carried by the rigid body 14, and is reported by the warning indicator 32 carried by the rigid body 14, all of them powered by the rechargeable battery 40 carried by the rigid body 14, the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 establishes the grip vacuum, monitors the grip vacuum, and activates the warning indicator 32 without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14. The whole chain, from the seal that is failing to the person who must act on it, is in the one hand that is holding the load.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.

In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on the state of the electric vacuum pump 20. When a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being configured to conform to and seal against a face of the panel under a clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: such panels are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 so as to establish the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.

At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At a comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At a maintaining step 212, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down. The placing step 202, the evacuating step 204, the monitoring step 206, the comparing step 208, the activating step 210, and the maintaining step 212 are all performed with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 unconnected to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

import re, glob, os, sys

base = "/home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p6"
os.chdir(base)

print("== figure brief sizes ==")
for f in sorted(glob.glob("figures/*.md")):
    t = open(f).read()
    print(os.path.basename(f), len(t))

print("== em dash / markers ==")
pats = ["—", "–", "TODO", "TBD", "DRAFTING NOTE", "please supply", "confirm", "placeholder"]
for f in sorted(glob.glob("draft/*.md")) + sorted(glob.glob("figures/*.md")):
    t = open(f).read()
    for p in pats:
        if p.lower() in t.lower():
            print("HIT", f, repr(p))

print("== numerals ==")
table = {}
for line in open("draft/numerals.md"):
    m = re.match(r"\|\s*(\d+)\s*\|\s*(.+?)\s*\|", line)
    if m:
        table[m.group(1)] = m.group(2)
spec = ""
for f in sorted(glob.glob("draft/0*.md")):
    spec += open(f).read() + "\n"
used = set(re.findall(r"\b(\d{2,3})\b", spec))
used = {u for u in used if u in table or True}
figs = {}
for f in sorted(glob.glob("figures/*.md")):
    t = open(f).read()
    tail = t.split("## Numerals shown on this figure")[-1]
    figs[os.path.basename(f)] = set(re.findall(r"^- (\d+)$", tail, re.M))
allfig = set().union(*figs.values())
print("table numerals:", len(table))
print("in table not on any figure:", sorted(set(table) - allfig, key=int))
print("on figure not in table:", sorted(allfig - set(table), key=int))
for k, v in figs.items():
    print(k, len(v), sorted(v, key=int))
# numerals used in spec text
spec_nums = set(n for n in re.findall(r"\b(\d{2,3})\b", spec) if n in table)
print("spec numerals not in table:", sorted(set(re.findall(r"\b(\d{2,3})\b", spec)) - set(table), key=int))
print("table numerals never used in spec:", sorted(set(table) - spec_nums, key=int))

print("== figure numeral-table vs list consistency ==")
for f in sorted(glob.glob("figures/*.md")):
    t = open(f).read()
    head = t.split("## Numerals shown on this figure")[0]
    tnums = set(re.findall(r"^\|\s*(\d+)\s*\|", head, re.M))
    tail = t.split("## Numerals shown on this figure")[-1]
    lnums = set(re.findall(r"^- (\d+)$", tail, re.M))
    if tnums != lnums:
        print("MISMATCH", f, sorted(tnums, key=int), sorted(lnums, key=int))
    # numerals mentioned in prose
    prose = set(re.findall(r"\b(\d{2,3})\b", head))
    prose = {p for p in prose if p in table}
    extra = prose - tnums
    if extra:
        print("PROSE-ONLY", f, sorted(extra, key=int))

print("== claim words missing from description ==")
claims = open("draft/09-claims.md").read()
rest = ""
for f in sorted(glob.glob("draft/0*.md")) + ["draft/10-abstract.md"]:
    if f.endswith("09-claims.md"):
        continue
    rest += open(f).read().lower() + "\n"
restwords = set(re.findall(r"[a-z]+", rest))
for i, block in enumerate(re.split(r"\n(?=\d+\. )", claims.strip())):
    num = block.split(".")[0]
    miss = sorted({w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", block.lower()) if w not in restwords})
    if miss:
        print("claim", num, miss)
