In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meaning. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which is placed against the workpiece 50.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create the grip vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air and so raises the grip vacuum, so that the grip vacuum retains a load on the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 shows the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40 schematically. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. What is monitored is the grip acting on the workpiece 50.

The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32. The warning indicator 32 is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost.

The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows a grip vacuum that is created and is subsequently lost.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first creates the grip vacuum, and the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the grip vacuum is lost, the grip vacuum trace 60 falls.

The warning indicator 32 is activated at a point on the falling grip vacuum trace 60. That point is marked on FIG. 4.

The warning indicator 32 is activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment that a person does not carry. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is held in the hand: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, before the load can be dropped, is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the load retained on the suction cup 10 is a glass or stone panel, and the workpiece 50 is a glass or stone panel. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 so as to create the grip vacuum. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.

At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum being lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate, while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load and before the load can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first establishes the grip vacuum, and the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls.

The grip vacuum is lost progressively as the grip vacuum trace 60 falls. The warning indicator 32 is activated at a point on the falling grip vacuum trace 60 at which the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped. That point is marked on FIG. 4.

This is the point of the arrangement. The user is told while the load is still held, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast, because the warning reaches the user while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

A device that treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected tells the user nothing about the grip, and if the leak is larger than the pump can make up the grip goes on decaying while the user is told nothing. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, before the load can be dropped, is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meaning. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which is placed against the workpiece 50.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create the grip vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air and so raises the grip vacuum, so that the grip vacuum retains a load on the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 shows the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40 schematically. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. What is monitored is the grip acting on the workpiece 50.

The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32. The warning indicator 32 is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost.

The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows a grip vacuum that is created and is subsequently lost.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first creates the grip vacuum, and the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the grip vacuum is lost, the grip vacuum trace 60 falls.

The warning indicator 32 is activated at a point on the falling grip vacuum trace 60. That point is marked on FIG. 4.

The warning indicator 32 is activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meaning. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which is placed against the workpiece 50.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create the grip vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air and so raises the grip vacuum, so that the grip vacuum retains a load on the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 shows the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40 schematically. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. What is monitored is the grip acting on the workpiece 50.

The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32. The warning indicator 32 is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost.

The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows a grip vacuum that is created and is subsequently lost.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first creates the grip vacuum, and the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the grip vacuum is lost, the grip vacuum trace 60 falls.

The warning indicator 32 is activated at a point on the falling grip vacuum trace 60. That point is marked on FIG. 4.

The warning indicator 32 is activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is held in the hand of the user, and the person holding the handle 16 is the one who acts on the warning.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the load retained on the suction cup 10 is that panel. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 so as to create the grip vacuum. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.

At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum being lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate, while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load and before the load can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meaning. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created by the electric vacuum pump 20 and monitored by the pressure sensor 30, expressed as a positive magnitude. The grip vacuum rises as air is removed by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as air leaks back. The grip vacuum is lost when air leaks back and the grip vacuum falls.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped by the suction cup 10 by way of a flexible sealing lip 12, and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section, taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1, through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The suction cup 10 comprises the flexible sealing lip 12, which is placed against the workpiece 50.

An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create the grip vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air and so raises the grip vacuum, so that the grip vacuum retains a load on the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 shows the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40 schematically. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. What is monitored is the grip acting on the workpiece 50.

The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32. The warning indicator 32 is configured to activate when the grip vacuum is lost.

The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The operation of the warning function is described with reference to FIG. 4, which plots grip vacuum on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows a grip vacuum that is created and is subsequently lost.

The electric vacuum pump 20 first creates the grip vacuum, and the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the grip vacuum is lost, the grip vacuum trace 60 falls.

The warning indicator 32 is activated at a point on the falling grip vacuum trace 60. That point is marked on FIG. 4.

The warning indicator 32 is activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is held in the hand of the user, and the person holding the handle 16 is the one who acts on the warning.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the load retained on the suction cup 10 is that panel. A glass or stone panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 so as to create the grip vacuum. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.

At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum being lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate, while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load and before the load can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

+The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is held in the hand of the user by way of the handle 16, and the warning indicator 32 warns the user before the load can be dropped.

input.summary: All sixteen findings are applied. The sealed region is gone as a numbered part, as a claim limitation, as a defined term and as a contact topology in the drawings: claim 1 now recites a suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip and a pump configured to draw air through a port to create a grip vacuum retaining a load, and the method claim places the lip against the workpiece and draws air through a port. The port no longer has a stated flow boundary, the warning indicator no longer has a stated mounting location, and the FIG. 4 trace no longer asserts a plateau or a monotonic decay. The panel-handling assertions, the clamping and lip-deflection mechanism, the enumerated leak causes, the comparative argument outside the Background, the set-down scenarios, the FIG. 1 staging, and the comparing-step decision loop are all removed, with claims 3 and 6 reduced to the glass or stone panel and the word planar deleted. Numeral 32 no longer marks an event on the FIG. 4 curve, the FIG. 2 caption no longer places anything but the pump and the port in the section, the dangling pronoun in the Summary is gone, and FIG. 1 now leads 14 inside the enclosure and 100 by a separate longer lead to the assembly. Numerals 18 and 208 were withdrawn with the structures they named, leaving eighteen numerals, each defined once, each used in the description, and each appearing on a sheet.
reasoning: Claim 1 was restored to the reviewer's wording, so the only structure it recites is what the inventor states: rigid body with a handle, suction cup with a flexible sealing lip, pump within the body drawing air through a port to create a grip vacuum that retains a load, sensor monitoring that grip vacuum, indicator driven by the sensor and activating when the grip vacuum is lost, and a rechargeable battery powering the pump.

Claim 3 recites the load retained on the suction cup rather than the workpiece, because deleting the sealed region removed the only appearance of a workpiece from claim 1 and the dependent claim would otherwise have lacked antecedent basis. The substance the review required, a glass or stone panel and nothing about planarity, is unchanged, and the method dependent keeps the workpiece wording since claim 4 introduces it in the preamble.

The description was cut to match. The grip vacuum is now defined as the vacuum created by the pump and monitored by the sensor, with no region and no boundary; the pump paragraph ends with the grip vacuum retaining a load; the FIG. 4 paragraphs state only that the trace rises and falls and that the activation point is marked; the comparative paragraphs about frame-mounted and pump-restart equipment are deleted, leaving the supported purpose statement that the indicator activates while the cup is still retaining the load, before the load can be dropped.

The one paragraph kept about the hand-held character of the tool was rewritten to say only what the disclosure says, that the lifter is held by the handle and the indicator warns the user before the load can be dropped, so no comparison to other equipment survives outside the Background.

Numeral 18 was withdrawn with the sealed region and numeral 208 with the comparing step, leaving eighteen numerals. FIG. 5 is now a straight column of four steps with no decision or feedback branch, and the description matches it step for step.

The figure briefs carry only the geometry the text supports. FIG. 1 no longer sets a panel attitude, a use scenario, finger clearance or a cup position, and gives 14 a broad interior target inside the enclosure while 100 gets a separate longer lead to the assembly clear of that outline. FIG. 2 shows the pump block and the aperture through which it draws air, with no sealed space, no port direction and no hatching topology. FIG. 4 carries three numerals and an unnumbered circle for the activation point, so numeral 32 again means one thing across the drawings.

draft/08-detailed-description.md: sealed region deleted throughout and the grip vacuum redefined without it; the port boundary sentence deleted; the warning indicator location sentence deleted; the lip deflection and atmospheric clamping clauses deleted; the enumerated leak causes replaced by a statement that the trace falls if the grip vacuum is lost; the frame-mounted and pump-restart comparison paragraphs deleted; the set-down scenarios deleted; the panel weight, attitude, loading and breakage clause deleted; the comparing step deleted from the method paragraphs.

draft/06-summary.md: sealed region and clamping removed from the opening paragraph, the comparative paragraph deleted in full, and the sentence with the dangling pronoun deleted so the warning paragraph reads as activation when the grip vacuum is lost while the cup is still retaining the load.
draft/10-abstract.md: sealed region removed, the suction cup recited as carrying a flexible sealing lip, and the closing sentence ended at before the load can be dropped.

draft/07-drawings.md: FIG. 1 caption recites the lip in contact with a workpiece; FIG. 2 caption now shows the electric vacuum pump and the port only; FIG. 4 caption no longer implies a decay profile.
draft/numerals.md: numerals 18 and 208 withdrawn, leaving eighteen entries.

figures/FIG-1: staging line, panel attitude, stack scenario, finger clearance, cup position and the warning indicator removed; separate lead instructions for 14 and 100; line 2-2 retained with both endpoints and arrow direction.
figures/FIG-2: sealed region bullet and numeral removed; the port bullet reduced to the aperture through which the pump draws air; the handle given a plain lead.
figures/FIG-4: trace bullets reduced to a curve that rises and falls; the activation point marked by an unnumbered circle; numeral 32 removed from the brief and from both numeral lists.
figures/FIG-5: comparing step and its feedback branch deleted, leaving four rectangles in a straight column with the activating step last.
input.prior_art_strategy: With the claims reduced to the inventor's own recitation, the distinction rests on the combination the disclosure states and on dependent claims 2 and 5: a cordless hand-held lifter whose electric pump sits within the rigid body, whose pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum, and whose warning indicator is driven by that sensor to activate when the grip vacuum is lost, while the suction cup is still retaining the load and before the load can be dropped. Removing the sealed region also removes the structure the Background attributes to US-10625955-B2, so the independent claims no longer track that reference's sealing units bounding a sealed space. Against US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, whose answer to a falling pressure is to restart the pump, and against WO-2017156581-A1, whose indicator confirms attachment above a safe level, claims 2 and 5 are the limitation that speaks to a grip being lost while the load is still held. US-10518985-B2 warns on a rate of vacuum change through a programmable controller; US-5310232-A and WO-2022236379-A1 are a suspended plate assembly and modules on a mounting frame rather than a tool carried in the hand; US-5374090-A indicates whether its power source is charged enough to grasp, computed from resistor voltage drops rather than from a vacuum measurement; US-5184858-A is manually pumped with no rechargeable battery; US-2024424646-A1 displays a negative pressure value for the operator to read; and CN-2806399-Y sounds a buzzer according to a usage state while pumping continuously. The Background sets out each of these teachings with its citation key, and nothing was added to the claims to improve that position beyond what the disclosure supports.
input.answer: Every listed finding has been applied. The sealed region, the port boundary statement, the indicator location, the FIG. 4 trace profile, the panel-handling assertions, the clamping and deflection mechanism, the leak causes, the comparative argument outside the Background, the set-down scenarios, the FIG. 1 staging, the comparing-step control loop, the double meaning of numeral 32, the FIG. 2 caption conflict, the dangling pronoun, the shared lead line in FIG. 1, and the word planar are all resolved. Six claims remain in two statutory classes, with claim 1 reciting the rigid body and handle, the suction cup with its flexible sealing lip, the electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body drawing air through a port to create a grip vacuum that retains a load, the pressure sensor monitoring it, the warning indicator driven by that sensor and activating when the grip vacuum is lost, and the rechargeable battery powering the pump; claims 2 and 5 add activation while the suction cup is still retaining the load, before the load can be dropped. The numeral table now holds eighteen numerals, each defined once, each used in the description, and each appearing on one of the five sheets, with no sheet carrying more than seven. No note, placeholder, question or instruction to a person appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/.
